sections.h2: Where is the Kalkaska County Register of Deeds?
sections.html:
The Register of Deeds works from the Administration Building at 605 N. Birch Street in the village of Kalkaska, MI 49646, and the phone number is 231-258-3315. The county page lists administration hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, and the office closes on legal holidays. The same counter handles passport applications by appointment, so call ahead if you need a time slot for something other than a quick drop off.

Kalkaska is a rural county in northern Lower Michigan, and Wikipedia describes it as part of the Traverse City metropolitan area. It covers 571 square miles, with over 80 lakes and about 275 miles of streams and rivers. Much of the land is marsh, and the Pere Marquette State Forest covers a large share of it.

Sellers with a cabin, a lake lot or acreage here record at this one office. Kalkaska is the only village in the county, and it is also the county seat.

sections.h2: What does recording cost in Kalkaska County?
sections.html:
Recording and indexing any deed, mortgage, lis pendens, affidavit or other instrument costs $30, no matter how many pages, a rule the county says began on October 1, 2016. Add $3 for each extra instrument number when a document discharges or assigns mortgages. The amounts follow MCL 600.2567.

A deed with a covenant of warranty, a land contract or an assignment of land contract needs a county treasurer tax certificate. The county charges $5.00 per instrument for up to five descriptions and 20 cents for every description after that. That matters in a county like this one, where a single sale can include several parcels.

  • Card payments run through the county's online payment page, which uses a paycode listed on the register of deeds page.
  • Plat books are sold in the office, for cash or check only.
  • A free property fraud alert notifies you of any document recorded with your name in it.

sections.h2: How much transfer tax does a Kalkaska County seller pay?
sections.html:
The seller pays state and county transfer tax at recording on any deed worth $100 or more. The rates are 55 cents per $500 for the county, in MCL 207.504, and $3.75 per $500 for the state. The county office publishes a chart so you can look up the figure for any price.

The deed has to state the value of the real estate on its face. Otherwise a real estate valuation affidavit goes in with it, at no filing fee, and the deed must mention that the affidavit is attached. Exemptions must be stated on the face of the deed too, under MCL 207.505 for the county and MCL 207.526 for the state.

sections.h2: Which Kalkaska County transfers are exempt from transfer tax?
sections.html:
Exemptions come straight from the two transfer tax acts, and the county posts both lists on its recording fees page. Instruments given as security, leases, and deeds from the government are exempt from both taxes. Transfers that merely confirm title already held, such as a quitclaim to fix a flaw, are exempt as well.

Family transfers differ. The state act exempts a conveyance from a person to a child, stepchild, grandchild or step-grandchild, and the county act has no such line. A deed in lieu of foreclosure or a foreclosure deed is also exempt from the state tax in MCL 207.526. A later resale by the entity that foreclosed is taxed normally.

Whichever exemption applies, write it on the face of the deed. If the county taxes a deed that should have been exempt, the seller can ask the state treasury for a refund under the state act.

sections.h2: Can I record a Kalkaska County deed electronically?
sections.html:
Yes. The county e-records every document type except judgments, court orders, plats, surveys and other certified documents. Its partner vendors are CSC, ePN, Indecomm and Simplifile, and warranty deeds, land contracts and other treasurer certified documents go through Simplifile only.

Title professionals can subscribe to Laredo, the county's records search program, by filling out a subscription agreement and sending it to the register of deeds. Individuals can use the free fraud alert and the front counter.

For a one time seller, the practical path is to let the title company or closing attorney e-record. If you want to bring a paper deed, check the formatting items in the next section first, since a rejected deed can push the closing back.

sections.h2: What formatting does Michigan require on a deed?
sections.html:
Every deed recorded in Michigan must meet MCL 565.201, and that applies in Kalkaska County as anywhere else. The register of deeds cannot take an instrument that misses an item. These points trip up homemade deeds most often:

  • A top margin of 2.5 inches on page one and half inch margins on the other sides.
  • Black ink on white paper of at least 20 pound weight, in 10 point type.
  • One statement on the first printed line naming the recordable event.
  • Printed names under each signature, with the notary name on the same page as the notary signature.
  • The grantee's address and the name and business address of the person who drafted the deed.
  • An English translation attached if any part is in another language.

The statute also says a recorded instrument is conclusively presumed to meet these rules, so a deed that gets through the counter stays on record even if a small error went unnoticed.

sections.h2: What do Kalkaska County housing numbers look like?
sections.html:
Kalkaska County is a small, mostly owner occupied market. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table puts the county at 18,693 residents in mid 2025, up 4.2 percent from the April 2020 base. There are 11,820 housing units, and 88.2 percent of occupied homes are owner occupied.

  • Median value of an owner occupied home: $188,900 for 2020 to 2024.
  • Median gross rent: $853 a month.
  • Residents aged 65 and older: 24.6 percent.
  • Average commute to work: 29.7 minutes, longer than in Jackson or Kalamazoo counties.
  • Population density: 32 people per square mile.

US 131 crosses the western part of the county, M-66 runs north and south through the west center, and M-72 runs east and west through the middle.

sections.h2: What should I line up before closing on a Kalkaska County sale?
sections.html:
Ask the county treasurer for a tax certificate and for the payoff on any unpaid property tax, and ask the register of deeds to confirm the paperwork. Ask the treasurer's office for current hours and the contact number before you go, since offices change schedules.

Settle with your title company which of the following it will cover, so nothing gets paid twice:

  • The $30 recording fee for the deed.
  • The treasurer's $5 tax certificate for up to five descriptions.
  • The combined transfer tax, which belongs to the seller.

If the sale includes several parcels, count the descriptions early, because each one past five adds 20 cents to the certificate.

faqs.q: What does the Kalkaska County Register of Deeds charge to record a deed?
faqs.a: It charges $30 per document, regardless of the number of pages. An extra $3 applies to each added instrument number when one document assigns or discharges several mortgages.

faqs.q: Does a Kalkaska County deed need a tax certificate?
faqs.a: Yes if it contains a covenant of warranty, or if it is a land contract or an assignment of land contract. The county treasurer's certificate costs $5.00 per instrument for up to five descriptions.

faqs.q: Who pays Kalkaska County transfer tax?
faqs.a: The seller pays. The county collects 55 cents and the state $3.75 per $500 of price when the deed is recorded, unless an exemption written on the deed applies.

faqs.q: Can I pay by card at the Kalkaska County Register of Deeds?
faqs.a: Yes. The register of deeds page links a county card payment service and gives a paycode to use. Treat the treasurer's tax certificate fee as a separate payment and ask that office how it takes payment.

faqs.q: What number do I call at the Kalkaska County Register of Deeds?
faqs.a: Call 231-258-3315. The office is at 605 N. Birch Street in Kalkaska and is open weekdays during administration hours.
